title: UK Post Office Horizon scandal: software evidence, institutional denial, and wrongful attribution to subpostmasters
summary: Horizon is promoted not as a simple bug case but as software plus legal/institutional attribution failure: unreliable or defective system state became evidence against people who could not see, challenge, or obtain decisive internal records on equal terms.

status_history.note: Promoted in rev0011 as part of the software accountability / attribution-trap lane.

place.event_context: United Kingdom Post Office branch network and legal/redress system

subjects.name: subpostmasters and others; not individually named in this record

claims.claim: The Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry Volume 1 report says Legacy Horizon was known by Fujitsu employees before rollout to be capable of producing false data because of bugs, errors and defects, and that senior and other Post Office employees knew or should have known while maintaining the fiction that Horizon data was always accurate.
what_would_change_status: A later inquiry volume changes the formulation of knowledge, timing, or institutional allocation.

claims.claim: The same inquiry volume says prosecutions and contractual liability relied on Horizon data asserted as reliable, and that many hundreds were wrongly convicted while many thousands were wrongly held responsible for illusory losses.

claims.claim: The Bates Horizon Issues judgment found a material risk that Horizon caused shortfalls, rejected the idea that this was extremely unlikely, and recorded that the system did not alert subpostmasters to relevant bugs/errors/defects.

type_payload.incident_class: software-plus-institutional evidence attribution and wrongful prosecution scandal
type_payload.system: Post Office Horizon accounting/branch IT system and associated audit/legal processes

sequence_of_events.event: Horizon was rolled out into branch accounting and contractual/prosecution contexts.
Bugs/errors/defects and false data capability existed and became contested through complaints, litigation, and inquiry.
Shortfalls were often attributed to subpostmaster error or dishonesty while critical audit data and disclosure were asymmetric.
Judgments, appeals, legislation, redress schemes, and statutory inquiry created correction-memory surfaces.

type_payload.proximate_cause: Software defects and evidence-access asymmetries became coupled to institutional/legal attribution of branch shortfalls to people rather than system state.

software_failure_fields.change_surface: branch accounting software treated as evidentiary infrastructure
software_failure_fields.validation_boundary: software defect detection, audit data, legal disclosure, branch reconciliation, institutional challenge process
software_failure_fields.blast_radius: hundreds wrongly convicted and many thousands held responsible for illusory losses according to Inquiry Volume 1
software_failure_fields.rollback_or_stop_authority: court judgments, appeal quashing, statutory inquiry, compensation/redress processes; full causal record still ongoing

software_accountability_fields.internal_state_surface: Horizon transaction, audit, keystroke, remote-access, bug/error/defect, and Fujitsu/Post Office knowledge surfaces
software_accountability_fields.external_attribution_surface: branch shortfalls, prosecutions, contractual claims, assumptions of human error or dishonesty
software_accountability_fields.investigation_or_detection_surface: Bates litigation, Hamilton appeal, CCRC referrals, public statutory inquiry, redress evidence
software_accountability_fields.corrective_or_legal_surface: Court of Appeal judgments, statutory inquiry, legislation/redress schemes, final archive transfer pending

contributing_factors: lack of branch alerting and audit access
latent_conditions: A software system used as evidentiary infrastructure can become machine testimony.
If the party asserting the software evidence controls logs, audit trails, and institutional interpretation, outsiders face an attribution trap.
